L314: Further consequences concern biased measures and weighted families [【47†42】], and the density of sunflower-free families of subspaces [【66†36】, 【67†46】]. The polynomial argument also connects to cap sets and tricolored sum-free sets [【52†19】, 【18†7】], while the set bound gives alternative exponential estimates for weak $\Delta$-systems, equidistant sets and odd sunflowers with an odd number of members [【42†45】, 【43†31】].
L315: The polynomial detector functions constructed in our proof also give subrank bounds with interpretations in matrix multiplication and exact entanglement conversion [【68†12】, 【69†55】]. Stronger conclusions would be needed for several further applications.
L316: In particular, one would need robust hitting estimates for lifting, circuit complexity, Kneser-graph packing and the Alon–Jaeger–Tarsi problem [【70†17】, 【40†4】], bounds independent of the ambient number of coordinates for random linear codes [【71†51】], and control of the core size for restricted-intersection and shadow-tomography problems [【72†37】].
L317: Harmonic least-common-multiple patterns. The following problem was posed by Erdős [【22†22】] (recorded as Problem 856 in Bloom’s collection [【73†8】]) in the same 1970 paper where the first mention of the Erdős-Szemerédi sunflower problem appears. Let $h_{k}(N)$ be the largest harmonic sum $\sum_{a\in A}1/a$ over sets $A\subseteq[N]$ containing no $k$ distinct integers whose pairwise least common multiples are all equal.
L318: Tang and Zhang establish a connection between this problem and sunflower-free set families [【45†52】]. Writing $\delta_{k}=1/(16k^{3})$, 【54†Theorem 1】 gives, for every fixed $k\geq 3$,
L319:  | $$h_{k}(N)\ll_{k}(\log N)^{1-\delta_{k}}.$$  |
L320: 
L321: Indeed, the squarefree-multiplier double count of Luo, Yang, and Zhu [【47†42】] gives
L322: 
L323:  | $$\left(\sum_{\begin{subarray}{c}q\leq N\\
L324: q\text{ squarefree}\end{subarray}}\frac{1}{q}\right)\sum_{a\in A}\frac{1}{a}\leq\sum_{u\leq N^{2}}\frac{F_{k}(\omega(u))}{u}\ll_{k}(\log N)^{2-\delta_{k}},$$  |
L325: where $F_{k}(r)$ denotes the maximum size of a $k$-sunflower-free family in $2^{[r]}$, and $\omega(u)$ counts the distinct prime divisors of $u$. The parenthesized sum is of order $\log N$, proving the claim. Thus we obtain a fixed logarithmic-power saving for every $k\geq 4$. For $k=3$, the Naslund–Sawin [【35†44】] bound already gives an asymptotic exponent $3/2^{2/3}-1=0.889881\ldots$ [【45†52】].
L326: There is also a Ramsey consequence. If $P$ is the product of the first $X$ primes, encode $S\subseteq[X]$ by $P/\prod_{i\in S}p_{i}$. A sunflower then gives integers with equal pairwise least common multiples. The monochromatic-sunflower estimate below and $\log P=O(X\log X)$ show that every $c$-coloring of $[N]$ contains such a monochromatic $k$-tuple once
L327: 
L328:  | $$N\geq\exp(A_{k}\log c\,\log\log c),$$  |
L329: 
L330: for a sufficiently large constant $A_{k}$ depending only on $k$ and all sufficiently large $c$.
L331: Equal subset sums. By 【54†Theorem 1】, every $c$-coloring of $2^{[N]}$ contains a monochromatic $k$-sunflower if
L332: 
L333:  | $$N>32k^{3}\log(3c).$$  |
L334: Indeed, a largest color class then has more than $3(2-\delta_{k})^{N}$ members. Coloring subsets of a sequence in a finite abelian group $G$ by their sums and cardinalities, and removing the common core, gives $k$ pairwise disjoint nonempty index sets of equal size and equal sum. Thus $A_{k}\log(2|G|)$ terms suffice, for a constant $A_{k}$ depending only on $k$. The cardinality color ensures that all petals have the same positive size.
L335: For three petals, this recovers the known consequence used by Alon, Shpilka and Umans to rule out the Coppersmith–Winograd conjecture about disjoint equivoluminous subsets [【16†2】].
L336: Similarly, a subset of $[M]$ of size at least $A_{k}\log(2M)$ contains $k$ pairwise disjoint nonempty subsets with a common positive sum $s$. To see this, color by sum and cardinality, using at most $(NM+1)(N+1)$ colors when the original set has size $N$. Taking unions gives $0,s,\ldots,ks$ among its subset sums. Both deductions apply for every fixed $k$.
L337: Induced Erdős–Sauer problem. As a final application, we mention a topic which has only recently been connected to sunflower problems. The famous Erdős–Sauer problem [【74†27】] asks, for fixed $k\geq 3$, for the maximum number of edges in an $n$-vertex graph not containing a $k$-regular subgraph. In a remarkable recent paper, Janzer and Sudakov [【75†38】] solved this problem by showing that the answer is $\Theta_{k}(n\log\log n)$, matching the lower bound of Pyber, Rödl and Szemerédi [【76†48】] from 1995.
L338: In a subsequent work, Chakraborti, Janzer, Methuku, and Montgomery [【77†11】] observed and used a connection between the Erdős-Sauer problem and the Erdős-Rado sunflower conjecture and obtained even essentially tight dependencies also on the regularity parameter $k$. None of these arguments, however, provide an induced $k$-regular subgraph. The induced variant of the problem, an arguably even more natural question, was already posed by Szemerédi in the 1970s; see Erdős [【74†27】, Section 3].
L339: Recently, we discovered a reduction showing that 【55†Theorem 2】 implies that $\Theta_{k}(n\log\log n)$ is the answer in the induced variant as well. Since the reduction is highly non-trivial and of a very different flavor from the arguments in this paper, we will present it in an upcoming short note [【78†10】].
L340: A recent preprint by Karingula and Lovett [【79†39】] proves that, for $k\geq 4$, every tensor faithfully realizing the set-sunflower relation on the full Boolean cube has maximal slice rank, over every field and with arbitrary nonzero values on the prescribed support. They also obtain comparable lower bounds when the relation is prescribed only on pairwise distinct inputs.
L341: They discuss extensive use of AI, including multi-agent setups, with particular emphasis on expressing their sunflower argument directly in terms of slice decompositions. Their obstruction concerns the set-sunflower relation. Our construction instead gives a tester for vector sunflowers, and we transfer the resulting vector bound to set families; thus their result does not directly apply to our tester.
L342: ### Statement on the use of AI
L343: The proof of 【55†Theorem 2】 was found by ChatGPT 6 Astra Pro, following a short discussion, which started by asking it to generalize the $k=3$ case argument in [【35†44】], which we needed for our original target of proving the induced variant of the Erdős–Sauer problem.
L344: The original argument it produced used the slice-rank terminology due to Tao (as used in [【35†44】]); we rewrote it in the polynomial method language as we believe this would make the argument slightly more approachable to a reader unfamiliar with the slice-rank method and since no deep result or property of slice rank was used. The authors have verified all the results in the paper and take full responsibility for the content.
L345: The proof has been verified in Lean 4.35; the verification will be made available on the Palomar repository.

L54: ### Our results
L55: 
L56: Firstly, we connect the sunflower number $\tau(\mathcal{F})$ and size of the family $\mathcal{F}$, and size of the shadow of the family $\partial\mathcal{F}$ in Section 【7†2】: in particular, we derive a lower bound on the size of the shadow. This result is again of independent interest and gives tighter bound than the Kruskal-Katona Theorem provided $\tau(\mathcal{F})\leq k$, for certain ranges of $k$. We have the following result in this direction.
L57: ###### Lemma 1.
L58: 
L59: $|\mathcal{F}|\leq\frac{\tau(\mathcal{F})}{k}*|\partial\mathcal{F}|$.
L60: Next, we study the Frankl’s $(i,j)$ shift/compression $\mathcal{C}_{ij}$ and study the variation of sunflower number under shift operations. Let $\mathcal{F}_{1,1}=\mathcal{F}$ and $\mathcal{F}_{i,j}=\mathcal{C}_{ij}(\mathcal{F}_{i,j-1})$, for $1\leq i<j\leq n$. Note that $\mathcal{F}_{n-1,n}$ is compressed: for any $F\in\mathcal{F}_{n-1,n}$, if $i\notin F$ and $j\in F$ and $i<j$, then $(F\setminus\{j\})\cup\{i\}\in\mathcal{F}_{n-1,n}$. It is not hard to see that $\mathcal{F}_{n-1,n}$ is also stable: i.e.
L61: $\mathcal{C}_{ij}(\mathcal{F}_{n-1,n})=\mathcal{F}_{n-1,n}$, for $1\leq i<j\leq n$ (see [【24†7】] for a proof). We define the operator $\mathcal{S}$ as a sequence of these $\binom{n}{2}$ shifts on some family $\mathcal{F}$ such that $\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{F})=\mathcal{F}_{n-1,n}$. We call a family shifted if $\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{F})=\mathcal{F}$.
L62: In Section 【8†3】, we provide an upper bound for the sunflower number of the shifted family, $\tau(\mathcal{S}(\mathcal{F}))$, in terms of the sunflower number of the original family, $\tau(\mathcal{F})$.

L77: ## 2 Sunflower Number and Shadows
L78: ###### Definition 1 (Shadow).
L79: 
L80: . Given a $k$-uniform set family $F$, the shadow $\partial F$ is defined as
L81: 
L82:  | $$\partial\mathcal{F}=\{E:E=F\setminus\{x\}\text{ for some }F\in\mathcal{F}\text{ and }x\in F\}.$$  |
L83: 
L84: ###### Statement of Lemma 1.
L85: 
L86: $|\mathcal{F}|\leq\frac{\tau(\mathcal{F})}{k}*|\partial\mathcal{F}|$.
L87: ###### Proof.
L88: 
L89: We prove the inequality by double-counting the number of pairs $(E,F)$ such that $F\in\mathcal{F}$, $E\in\partial\mathcal{F}$, and $E\subset F$. Let this quantity be $N$.
L90: 
L91: First, we calculate $N$ by summing over the sets in $\mathcal{F}$. Since $\mathcal{F}$ is $k$-uniform, every set $F\in\mathcal{F}$ contains exactly $\binom{k}{k-1}=k$ subsets of size $k-1$. By the definition of the shadow, all such subsets belong to $\partial\mathcal{F}$. Thus, each $F$ contributes exactly $k$ to the sum:
L92:  | $$N=\sum_{F\in\mathcal{F}}k=k\cdot|\mathcal{F}|\quad(*)$$  |
L93: 
L94: Next, we calculate $N$ by summing over the sets in the shadow $\partial\mathcal{F}$. For each $E\in\partial\mathcal{F}$, let $d_{\mathcal{F}}(E)$ denote the number of sets in $\mathcal{F}$ that contain $E$ (often called the codegree or extension degree of $E$).
L95: 
L96:  | $$N=\sum_{E\in\partial\mathcal{F}}d_{\mathcal{F}}(E)$$  |
L97: 
L98: Consider the family of extensions of a specific set $E\in\partial\mathcal{F}$:
L99:  | $$\mathcal{F}_{E}=\{F\in\mathcal{F}:E\subset F\}$$  |
L100: Since any distinct $F_{i},F_{j}\in\mathcal{F}_{E}$ share exactly the set $E$ (as $|F|=k$ and $|E|=k-1$, they can only differ by one element), the family $\mathcal{F}_{E}$ forms a sunflower with kernel $E$ and petals of size 1. The size of this sunflower is exactly $|\mathcal{F}_{E}|=d_{\mathcal{F}}(E)$.By definition, $\tau(\mathcal{F})$ is the size of the largest sunflower in $\mathcal{F}$. Therefore, for every $E\in\partial\mathcal{F}$, we must have:
L101: 
L102:  | $$d_{\mathcal{F}}(E)\leq\tau(\mathcal{F})$$  |
L103: Substituting this bound into our summation for $N$:
L104: 
L105:  | $$N=\sum_{E\in\partial\mathcal{F}}d_{\mathcal{F}}(E)\leq\sum_{E\in\partial\mathcal{F}}\tau(\mathcal{F})=\tau(\mathcal{F})\cdot|\partial\mathcal{F}|\quad(**)$$  |
L106: 
L107: Combining $(*)$ and $(**)$:
L108: 
L109:  | $$k\cdot|\mathcal{F}|\leq\tau(\mathcal{F})\cdot|\partial\mathcal{F}|$$  |

L4@P0: Abstract
L5@P0: Robust Sunflower lemmas imply that any large enough monotone DNF of width w
L6@P0: contains a sunflower, i.e., a DNF equivalent to the conjunction of a common core with
L7@P0: a DNF that is heavily biased towards 1. While these lemmas are typically proved in
L8@P0: the context of the uniform distribution or i.i.d. distributions, they also hold for O(w
L9@P0: 2
L10@P0: )-
L11@P0: wise independent distributions by Bazzi’s theorem (Bazzi (SICOMP 2009); Tal (CCC
L12@P0: 2017)), which states that width-w DNFs cannot distinguish between such distributions
L13@P0: and the uniform distribution.
L14@P0: We prove a derandomization of robust sunflower lemmas for O(w)-wise independent
L15@P0: distributions, which recovers the derandomization above with slightly weaker parameters. Notably, our result also holds for distributions whose marginals are “locally
L16@P0: independent” and “approximately identically” distributed. It is not known whether
L17@P0: such distributions fool general DNFs, which makes the derandomization via DNFfooling techniques unavailable. Our proof of this derandomization is via the method
L18@P0: of moments, which might be of independent interest.
L19@P0: We apply this result to obtain improved separations between non-monotone arithmetic circuits and the radical of monotone circuits. Specifically, we construct an explicit
L20@P0: family of multilinear polynomials Pn that have small non-monotone arithmetic circuits
L21@P0: such that any power of Pn cannot be computed by monotone arithmetic circuits of
L22@P0: sub-exponential size. This improves on a recent result of Cavalar, Fabris, Mukhopadhyay, Srinivasan and Yehudayoff (STOC 2026), who proved a non-explicit separation
L23@P0: that was quasipolynomial. Our construction uses Nisan-Wigderson designs with an
L24@P0: additional linear-algebraic expansion property.

L56@P2: 1.1 Background and Results
L57@P2: The sunflower lemma of Erd˝os and Rado [ER60] states that every large enough family of
L58@P2: sets must contain a sunflower : a family of sets whose pairwise intersections are identical. Along the decades, this elegant definition has found applications in several areas of
L59@P2: theoretical computer science, including circuit complexity [Raz85, HJP95], data structure
L60@P2: lower bounds [FMS93, RR18], matrix multiplication algorithms [ASU13], parametrized
